quiz.q: A 3-year-old has a barky cough and audible stridor while sitting quietly on his mother's lap. SpO2 is 95 percent. What is the most appropriate triage action?
choices: Obtain a throat swab to rule out streptococcal infection before assigning a level
Take him from his mother to a treatment room for a full examination
Assign ESI 2, keep him on his mother's lap, and minimize anything that upsets him
Assign ESI 4 since his oxygen saturation is normal
quiz.why: Stridor at rest means significant upper airway narrowing, and agitation increases turbulent flow and can worsen obstruction. A throat examination or separating him from his parent both risk provoking that, and a normal saturation is a late-failing measure in airway narrowing.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old is brought in intoxicated, rousable, with a GCS of 15 when awake and no obvious injury. Which triage decision is safest?
choices: ESI 4 in a lobby chair until he sobers up
ESI 5, since no resources are expected
ESI 3 with a glucose, monitoring and serial reassessment
ESI 2 with a monitored bed and a sitter for every intoxicated patient
quiz.why: Intoxication masks head injury, hypoglycemia, infection and withdrawal, and attributing altered mentation to alcohol is the classic miss. A lobby chair provides no serial assessment, and reflexively assigning ESI 2 to every intoxicated patient would consume monitored beds without a high-risk feature.

quiz.q: A 29-year-old states he has a specific suicide plan and purchased the means yesterday. He is calm, polite and fully oriented with normal vital signs. What is correct?
choices: His calm presentation supports a lower acuity with outpatient referral
ESI 3, because the resource count includes a psychiatric consultation and labs
ESI 1, because suicidal ideation always requires immediate life-saving intervention
ESI 2 with immediate safety measures, because plan plus preparatory behavior is high risk
quiz.why: Plan and preparatory behavior are the highest-risk elements on any suicide screen, and a settled affect in a patient who has decided is a recognized danger sign rather than reassurance. Resource counting never occurs once the high-risk gate fires, and ESI 1 requires an intervention happening at that moment.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old arrives after two days of vomiting. Which systolic blood pressure defines hypotension at this age?
choices: Under 80
Under 90
Under 70
Under 60
quiz.why: From 1 to 10 years, the threshold is 70 plus twice the age in years, which gives 80 at age 5. Ninety applies over 10 years, 70 applies to infants, and 60 applies to term neonates.

quiz.q: A 10-month-old has had diarrhea for three days. He has dry lips, no tears, sunken eyes, a capillary refill of 3 seconds and one wet diaper in 20 hours. How should this be graded and triaged?
choices: Mild dehydration, roughly 3 to 5 percent, suitable for oral fluids in the lobby
Moderate dehydration, roughly 6 to 9 percent, warranting prompt evaluation
Severe dehydration, since one wet diaper always means 10 percent or more
Not gradable without a recent weight to compare against
quiz.why: Dry membranes, absent tears, sunken eyes and a refill of 2 to 3 seconds define moderate dehydration. Severe requires refill over 3 seconds with mottling and lethargy, and dehydration is routinely graded on clinical findings when no recent weight exists.

quiz.q: A 4-month-old with bronchiolitis begins grunting with each exhalation while you are obtaining vitals. What does this indicate?
choices: Nasal congestion requiring suction before any other action
A normal infant sound associated with feeding and settling
Upper airway obstruction that should be managed like croup
Expiration against a partly closed glottis to maintain airway pressure, a sign of significant distress
quiz.why: Grunting is self-generated positive pressure against collapsing alveoli and is the most ominous respiratory sound in a child. Stridor indicates upper airway narrowing, and suctioning does not address collapse at the alveolar level.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old with a known asthma exacerbation was wheezing loudly on arrival. Twenty minutes later his chest is quiet and he is sleepy. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The quiet chest means too little air is moving, and he needs immediate attention
He is improving and can be moved down the recheck list
Sleepiness after albuterol is expected and reassuring
The wheeze resolved, so he can be reclassified as ESI 4
quiz.why: A silent chest in a known wheezer means airflow has fallen below the level needed to generate sound, which is a pre-arrest finding. Drowsiness in that setting suggests rising carbon dioxide rather than a calm child responding to treatment.

quiz.q: A parent reports giving ibuprofen two hours before arrival. The child's temporal temperature at triage is 37.1 C. What should you do?
choices: Chart afebrile and proceed with a low acuity
Ask what was given, the dose and the exact time, chart it, and use an accurate route
Repeat the temporal reading in 10 minutes to confirm
Assume the parent is mistaken since the reading is normal
quiz.why: Antipyretics mask fever for hours, so a normal reading afterward is not evidence the child was never febrile, and temporal readings additionally miss fevers. Repeating an inaccurate route or doubting the parent adds nothing to the decision.

quiz.q: A 76-year-old on metoprolol looks pale and clammy. HR 86, BP 104/60. His wife says his pressure runs around 160/90. How should this be read?
choices: Normal vitals for age, no escalation needed
Concerning only once the heart rate exceeds 100
Blunted tachycardia plus a large relative fall in pressure, which is concerning for shock
Expected medication effect requiring no note in the chart
quiz.why: Beta blockade caps the compensatory heart rate response, so 86 may be his ceiling, and a 56 mmHg drop from his own baseline is a major change. Waiting for a rate over 100 in a beta-blocked patient means waiting for a sign that may never come.

quiz.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident is brought in for altered mental status. Temperature is 36.1 C, HR 94, BP 110/64, RR 22. Which statement is correct?
choices: The absence of fever argues strongly against infection
Altered mental status in this age group is usually baseline dementia
The normal blood pressure excludes a perfusion problem
Hypothermia and a respiratory rate over 20 with new confusion meet sepsis screen criteria
quiz.why: Temperature under 36.0 C counts as a sepsis criterion alongside fever, and older adults with serious infection are frequently afebrile or hypothermic. Assuming dementia without asking about baseline is the mechanism of the miss, and a normal-range pressure can still be a large relative drop.

quiz.q: A 71-year-old on apixaban tripped on a rug, struck his forehead, and did not lose consciousness. He is alert with a small abrasion and normal vitals. What is the correct triage consideration?
choices: Anticoagulation plus a head strike is its own risk category with potentially delayed presentation
Ground-level falls are low-energy and do not raise acuity
Absence of loss of consciousness effectively excludes intracranial bleeding
The size of the abrasion determines the level
quiz.why: Anticoagulated patients bleed intracranially after minor trauma, often without loss of consciousness and with symptoms delayed by hours to days. Ground-level falls in older adults produce serious injury at rates comparable to high-energy mechanisms in the young, and external wound size predicts nothing about the brain.

quiz.q: Which question best separates delirium from dementia at the triage desk?
choices: Do you know what year it is?
Has she ever been diagnosed with memory problems?
Is this how she was last week, and does it come and go?
Can she still dress and feed herself?
quiz.why: Delirium is defined by acute onset and a fluctuating course, so timing and baseline are the discriminators. Orientation questions, a prior diagnosis and functional status describe current or chronic state without establishing when the change began.

quiz.q: A 79-year-old man's only complaint is weakness. He has no chest pain and his vitals are HR 58 and BP 112/64. What should happen at triage?
choices: Assign ESI 4 and place him in the lobby since he has no specific complaint
Obtain only a point-of-care glucose and wait for the provider
Obtain a 12-lead EKG, because weakness in an older patient is an anginal equivalent
Assign ESI 5 since no resources are anticipated
quiz.why: Weakness, dizziness, syncope and epigastric pain are all anginal equivalents in older and diabetic patients, and a 12-lead is a standing order for them. Bradycardia at 58 is itself a clue to an inferior infarct, and a glucose alone does not address the cardiac question.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old restrained driver arrives after a moderate-speed crash. His systolic blood pressure is 104 and he is alert. Which is correct?
choices: No criterion is met because 104 exceeds the adult threshold of 90
Restraint use removes him from activation criteria
Only a partial activation applies because he is alert
A systolic under 110 after age 65 may represent shock and typically triggers full activation
quiz.why: Current field and ED triage criteria lower the shock threshold to 110 systolic after age 65 because older adults are systematically undertriaged. Neither restraint use nor an alert appearance cancels a criterion that has already been met.

quiz.q: A patient walks into triage from a rollover crash in which another occupant died. He looks well and has normal vital signs. What applies?
choices: The mechanism criterion of a death in the same compartment is met and triggers activation
No activation, since he is ambulatory with normal vitals
Activation depends solely on his Glasgow Coma Scale
He should be triaged ESI 4 and rechecked hourly
quiz.why: Activation is triggered by mechanism and numbers, not by appearance at the door, and death in the same compartment is a standard mechanism criterion. Looking well after a high-energy mechanism is common early and is exactly what mechanism criteria exist to override.

quiz.q: During a trauma resuscitation you have finished cutting off the patient's clothing. What is the immediate next priority in your role?
choices: Bag and label the clothing before anything else
Cover the patient with warm blankets, because hypothermia feeds the lethal triad
Move to the head of the bed to help with the airway
Leave the patient exposed until the secondary survey is finished
quiz.why: Hypothermia impairs clotting and joins acidosis and coagulopathy in the lethal triad, so rewarming starts as soon as exposure is complete. Clothing can be handled a moment later, drifting to the head of the bed interferes with airway roles, and prolonged exposure is a preventable harm.

quiz.q: A gunshot victim's shirt has a defect over the entry wound. How should you remove and store it?
choices: Cut through the defect to speed removal and use a plastic bag
Cut around the defect and place the shirt in a paper bag per policy
Pull the shirt over his head intact and hand it to family
Discard it with the other trauma waste
quiz.why: Cutting through a defect destroys information about range and trajectory, and plastic traps moisture that degrades biological evidence. Pulling clothing over the head risks spinal movement and evidence loss, and discarding it breaks the chain entirely.

quiz.q: A massive transfusion protocol is activated and you are assigned the cooler. Which action is correct?
choices: Open the cooler and lay out all units on the counter so they are ready
Warm all units in a sink of hot water before use
Hand the cooler to the first available person without documentation
Keep the cooler closed, document unit numbers, and return unused units promptly
quiz.why: Blood products must stay within a temperature range and be traceable to a specific patient, so the cooler stays closed and every unit is documented and accounted for. Laying units out, improvising warming, or handing the cooler off untracked all risk wasted product or a transfusion error.

quiz.q: A patient answers yes to the ASQ acuity question about having suicidal thoughts right now. What happens next?
choices: Treat it as an acute positive: the patient is not left alone and the nurse is told immediately
Document it and continue the routine triage sequence
The tech assigns a risk level based on the total number of yes answers
Repeat the screen in one hour to see whether the answer changes
quiz.why: A yes to current suicidal thoughts is an acute positive requiring continuous observation and immediate escalation. The tech may administer the screen where policy allows but never determines risk, and delaying to repeat the screen leaves a high-risk patient unobserved.

quiz.q: While searching a behavioral health patient's bag you find a folding knife. What do you do?
choices: Remove it, wrap it in a towel, and place it in the belongings bag
Leave it, keep line of sight, and call security without handling the weapon
Hand it to the patient's family member in the waiting room
Carry it to the nurses station and lock it in a drawer
quiz.why: Handling a weapon puts it in motion and puts you within reach of it, so policy is to stop, maintain observation and call security. Giving it to family or moving it yourself also breaks the chain of custody if the item becomes evidence.

quiz.q: Which restraint practice meets current standards?
choices: Prone positioning with pressure across the upper back to control movement
Supine positioning with circulation, skin and needs checked at least every 15 minutes
Applying restraints to a verbally abusive but non-threatening patient
Leaving the order open-ended until psychiatry arrives
quiz.why: Prone restraint with weight on the back causes positional asphyxia and is prohibited. Restraint requires imminent danger rather than rudeness, and federal rules require timed orders, a face-to-face evaluation within an hour, and checks at least every 15 minutes.

quiz.q: A patient on an involuntary hold in New Jersey tells you he is leaving and walks toward the ambulance bay. What is correct?
choices: He may leave, since a screening certificate is only a recommendation
Let him go and document that he left against medical advice
Physically restrain him yourself before telling anyone
Notify staff and security immediately; a patient on a hold may not leave and elopement is an emergency
quiz.why: A screening certificate is a legal hold, so the patient may not leave and an elopement is called at once. Documenting it as leaving against medical advice misstates his legal status, and restraint is a team action with a provider order, never a solo improvisation.

quiz.q: Which triage note entry best meets documentation standards?
choices: Odor of alcohol, unsteady gait, states 'I had six beers,' declined a repeat blood pressure
Patient is drunk, uncooperative and a frequent flyer
Intoxicated, no acute distress, here to sleep it off
Drug seeking, demanding intravenous medication
quiz.why: Observations and direct quotations are facts that survive later review, while labels are conclusions that must be defended and that bias every clinician who reads the chart afterward.

quiz.q: You realize an hour later that you charted the wrong last known well time on a stroke patient. What do you do?
choices: Edit the original entry so the record is accurate
Enter an addendum with its own timestamp stating the correction and the source
Leave it alone and tell the nurse verbally
Delete the note and re-enter the whole triage assessment
quiz.why: Corrections are made by addendum with an independent timestamp so the record shows what was known and when. Editing or deleting an original entry destroys the credibility of the entire chart, and a verbal correction alone leaves the wrong time driving treatment decisions.

quiz.q: A man collapses in the hospital parking lot 100 yards from the entrance. A clerk says he is not registered so he is not a patient. What is correct?
choices: He is not an ED patient until he presents at the desk
EMTALA obligations extend to hospital property, generally within 250 yards, so he is an ED patient
Emergency services must be called and the hospital should not intervene
He becomes a patient only once insurance is verified
quiz.why: The obligation to provide a medical screening examination extends to hospital property, generally including areas within 250 yards of the main building. Registration status and insurance verification have no bearing on whether the duty exists.

quiz.q: The lobby holds 38 patients and the department is boarding 12 admissions. Which practice is the one that must not be dropped?
choices: Full registration before any clinical contact
Placing every low-acuity patient in a bed rather than a chair
Waiting for a bed before performing any standing-order testing
Documented waiting room reassessment at the interval for each acuity level
quiz.why: Reassessment is the safety net under every triage decision and is the first thing to silently disappear under load. Full registration may be deferred to quick registration, split flow deliberately keeps low-acuity patients vertical, and standing-order testing is meant to happen before a bed exists.

scenarios.title: Seven weeks old, and he feels warm
scenarios.intro: It is 0230 on a Tuesday. A mother carries in a 7-week-old boy wrapped in two blankets. She says he felt warm at bedtime and has been fussy, then sleepy. He was born at 39 weeks with no complications. The lobby holds four other patients and one main-side bed is open.

steps.prompt: She hands you the baby at the triage window. He is swaddled tightly and quiet. What is your first move?

choices.text: Unwrap him and look at him before asking any questions: color, tone, breathing, responsiveness.
choices.feedback: Correct. The across-the-room look in an infant means seeing skin and chest wall. A swaddled baby hides mottling, retractions and tone, and those are the three things that matter most.

choices.text: Start the interview: onset, feeding, wet diapers, sick contacts.
choices.feedback: The history matters, but not before you look. A history taken over a swaddled infant can go five minutes without anyone noticing that the baby is gray.

choices.text: Put a temporal thermometer across his forehead to get a fast number.
choices.feedback: Temporal readings miss fevers, and under 3 months the reference standard is rectal. A falsely normal temporal reading here could lower the acuity on a neonate who needs a full workup.

steps.prompt: Unwrapped, he is pale with mottled knees. He has mild subcostal retractions and does not fix on your face. Rectal temperature is `38.4 C`. You have a full set.

choices.text: Tell the triage nurse now: 7 weeks old, rectal 38.4, mottled, retracting, heart rate 186, not fixing on faces.
choices.feedback: Correct. Every element of that sentence is a decision driver, and you delivered age, route, temperature, appearance and numbers in one breath.

choices.text: Finish the registration questions, then report.
choices.feedback: Registration is not a gate. An infant at this age with this temperature and appearance is a high-acuity patient before anyone types a name.

choices.text: Re-swaddle him to keep him warm and place them in the lobby with a 30-minute recheck.
choices.feedback: A febrile infant under 90 days is not a lobby patient. Re-swaddling also hides the exact findings the nurse needs to see herself.

choices.text: Weigh him in kilograms and recheck the heart rate while you page the nurse.
choices.feedback: Reasonable and the weight will be needed for every dose, but the report should not wait behind a second measurement in a mottled infant.

steps.prompt: The nurse assigns ESI 2 and takes the open main-side bed. She asks you to get the room ready while she calls the provider. The mother says: 'He is my first. Is this bad?'

choices.text: Say that his temperature is high for his age so the team needs to check him quickly and thoroughly, and that you will stay with them.
choices.feedback: Correct. Honest, non-technical, and it does not promise an outcome. Naming the reason for the urgency reduces panic rather than causing it.

choices.text: Tell her not to worry, babies get fevers all the time.
choices.feedback: False reassurance. If this becomes a spinal tap and an admission in twenty minutes, she will stop believing anything else anyone says.

choices.text: Tell her the baby may be septic and will likely need a lumbar puncture and antibiotics.
choices.feedback: That is the provider's conversation, not yours, and it delivers a diagnosis the team has not made yet.

choices.text: Say you cannot answer that but the nurse will be right in.
choices.feedback: Safe but hollow. You can honestly explain the urgency without giving a diagnosis, and doing so is part of the job.

steps.prompt: The provider orders blood and urine studies, a lumbar puncture tray, and antibiotics. She wants the antibiotic as soon as the cultures are obtained. What is the correct sequence for your part?

choices.text: Set up for the blood culture and other labs first so the specimen is obtained before antibiotics are given.
choices.feedback: Correct. A culture drawn after antibiotics may never identify the organism, and this is the one step in the sequence a tech can personally ruin.

choices.text: Hang the antibiotic first since time to antibiotics is the quality measure.
choices.feedback: The measure is fast antibiotics after cultures, not instead of them. Losing the organism costs this baby a targeted drug for the rest of the admission.

choices.text: Set up the lumbar puncture tray first and let the blood work follow.
choices.feedback: The tray needs to be ready, but the blood culture is the time-critical specimen relative to the antibiotic, and it is the one you control.

scenarios.debrief: Three rules decided this case and none of them required an opinion about the diagnosis. First, look at a baby with the blanket off, because appearance, work of breathing and skin are the pediatric assessment, and a swaddle hides all three. Second, under 90 days the route is rectal and the age plus temperature rule drives the acuity regardless of how well the infant looks. Third, cultures before antibiotics: the sepsis bundle rewards speed, but a culture drawn after the first dose can leave the team treating blind for days. The sentence you gave the nurse, age plus route plus temperature plus appearance plus numbers, is the format worth memorizing for every escalation you will ever make.

scenarios.title: He drove himself in from the rollover
scenarios.intro: A 24-year-old man walks up to the triage window holding his left side. He says his truck rolled twice on a county road about forty minutes ago, he climbed out through the window, and a friend drove him here. His shirt is torn and there is glass in his hair. He is talking in full sentences and wants to know how long the wait is.

steps.prompt: He looks uninjured apart from an abrasion on his left forearm. What is the most important thing to establish right now?

choices.text: The mechanism in detail: rollover, ejection or self-extrication, other occupants, intrusion, speed, restraint use.
choices.feedback: Correct. Activation criteria are written in mechanism and numbers, and the mechanism is the only thing that will be unavailable later if you do not capture it now.

choices.text: His pain score, so the severe-pain gate can be applied.
choices.feedback: Pain matters but does not decide this. A young patient can be minimally symptomatic with a splenic injury, and the mechanism is what overrides how well he looks.

choices.text: Whether he has insurance and a primary care doctor, so registration is complete.
choices.feedback: Registration never precedes the screening examination, and none of it bears on whether this patient meets trauma criteria.

steps.prompt: He says the truck rolled twice, he was belted, the roof came down onto the passenger seat, and his passenger was taken by helicopter. His only complaint is left-sided rib pain when he breathes deeply.

choices.text: Report the mechanism to the nurse immediately: rollover, significant roof intrusion, another occupant flown out, left rib pain, heart rate 104.
choices.feedback: Correct. Roof intrusion and a critically injured co-occupant are standard mechanism criteria, and left rib pain plus a rising heart rate is a spleen story until proven otherwise.

choices.text: Assign him a lobby chair with a recheck at 30 minutes, since he is ambulatory with stable vitals.
choices.feedback: Ambulatory and talking is exactly how young trauma patients present before they decompensate. He met mechanism criteria before he reached the window.

choices.text: Get a full set of vitals repeated, then decide whether to escalate.
choices.feedback: Repeat vitals are useful, but the mechanism already met criteria. Escalate first, measure while you wait.

choices.text: Bring him to a bed and start cutting off his clothing before telling anyone.
choices.feedback: The bed is right, but undressing a trauma patient alone in a room without an activation means nobody else knows he is there.

steps.prompt: A partial trauma activation is called. In the bay, the team is arriving. The nurse asks you to expose the patient and get him on the monitor. He says he is cold and asks you to leave his jeans on.

choices.text: Explain that everything comes off so nothing is missed, remove it, then cover him with warm blankets immediately.
choices.feedback: Correct. Full exposure then immediate rewarming. Hypothermia joins acidosis and coagulopathy in the lethal triad, and a hidden posterior wound is exactly what exposure finds.

choices.text: Leave the jeans on since his complaint is thoracic and he is alert.
choices.feedback: Injuries hide under clothing, particularly on the back and in the groin and axillae. The alert patient with a distracting rib injury is the classic missed-injury case.

choices.text: Remove everything and leave him uncovered so the team can complete the survey.
choices.feedback: Exposure is right, prolonged uncovering is not. Cover between survey steps; it costs nothing and protects clotting.

choices.text: Cut the jeans off along the seams and place the clothing in a bag for the family.
choices.feedback: Reasonable technique. Just do not let bagging delay the blanket, and follow policy on how clothing is stored.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes in, he becomes quiet and asks for water. You take a repeat set.

choices.text: Say the numbers out loud to the team now: heart rate up from 104 to 128, pressure down to 98 over 58, and he has gone quiet.
choices.feedback: Correct. Trend plus behavior change, delivered as a sentence. A patient who stops talking has not improved, and the team needs the delta, not just the current number.

choices.text: Chart the vitals and give him a cup of water since he is asking.
choices.feedback: Nothing by mouth in a trauma patient who may go to the operating room, and charting a trend without saying it out loud is how deterioration goes unnoticed in a busy bay.

choices.text: Recheck the pressure manually before reporting anything.
choices.feedback: Verification is a good habit, but not in a trauma bay with a rising heart rate. Report, then verify while the team responds.

steps.prompt: The team escalates to a full activation and calls for the ultrasound and blood. What is your most useful next action?

choices.text: Get the ultrasound in position with gel, confirm large-bore access is in, and be ready to run the type and screen and get the cooler.
choices.feedback: Correct. Anticipating the next three things the team will need is the whole job in a resuscitation.

choices.text: Start a detailed secondary survey of his extremities.
choices.feedback: That belongs to the clinicians and it is not the priority while a hemorrhage question is open.

choices.text: Go find the family to update them.
choices.feedback: Family communication matters and is not yours to do mid-resuscitation, and leaving the bay removes a pair of hands.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern here is the walk-in trauma, and it beats appearance every time. Activation criteria are written in mechanism and numbers precisely because young patients compensate: roof intrusion and a critically injured co-occupant met criteria before anyone measured a blood pressure. The second pattern is the trend. A single heart rate of 104 means little; 104 rising to 128 with a falling pressure and a patient who has gone quiet is a hemorrhage narrative, and saying the delta out loud is what converts data into action. The third is exposure and rewarming as one motion rather than two: everything off so nothing is missed, blankets on immediately because hypothermia is the part of the lethal triad you personally control.

scenarios.title: Nine from the bus, four open beds
scenarios.intro: At 1610 the charge nurse announces an incoming notification: a transit bus struck a utility pole two miles away. Nine patients are being transported to your department, with three more going elsewhere. You have four open beds, a full lobby, and six admitted patients boarding. You are one of two techs on the main side.

steps.prompt: The charge nurse tells the team to prepare. Before any patient arrives, what is the highest-value thing you can do?

choices.text: Create capacity and stage supplies: move discharge-ready patients out, strip and turn over rooms, stage trauma trays, IV setups and blood tubes.
choices.feedback: Correct. Capacity and staged supplies are the two things that cannot be created after patients start arriving. This is the surge equivalent of setting up the bay.

choices.text: Go to the ambulance bay and wait to help unload.
choices.feedback: Well intentioned, but a tech standing in the bay is a tech not creating the beds those patients need. Unloading is usually staffed separately.

choices.text: Start calling family members of boarding patients to arrange rides.
choices.feedback: Discharge flow matters but this is not your call to make unilaterally, and phone calls consume the minutes that room turnover needs.

steps.prompt: The first three patients arrive together. One is walking and crying, one is on a backboard with an obvious open forearm fracture, and one is on a stretcher breathing at 36 with cool skin and no radial pulse. Triage is using START at the door.

choices.text: Identify the third as red, the second as yellow, and the walking patient as green, and say it to the triage nurse.
choices.feedback: Correct. Respirations over 30 and an absent radial pulse both make red. Walking makes green regardless of how upset the patient is. An isolated fracture with intact perfusion and mentation is yellow.

choices.text: Treat the open fracture first because it looks the worst.
choices.feedback: Appearance is not acuity. The dramatic injury is yellow and the quiet one on the stretcher is the red.

choices.text: Assign the crying walking patient a bed since she is clearly distressed.
choices.feedback: Distress is real but ambulatory patients are green in START, and the single highest-yield step in a surge is moving all of them to one designated area.

choices.text: Ask the triage nurse which one she wants you to take first.
choices.feedback: Acceptable in a calm department, but in a surge everyone is deciding at once. Knowing the sort yourself is what makes you useful.

steps.prompt: A police officer tells you two of the incoming patients were sprayed with a chemical from a ruptured container on the bus and are still wet. They are three minutes out.

choices.text: Tell the charge nurse immediately and make sure they are decontaminated outside before entering the building.
choices.feedback: Correct. Contamination brought through the doors closes the department and injures staff. Decontamination happens outside, without exception.

choices.text: Bring them straight into two rooms and close the doors.
choices.feedback: This contaminates the corridor and the rooms, and exposes everyone on the way in. Closed doors do not undo a contaminated path.

choices.text: Put masks on them and route them through the ambulance entrance.
choices.feedback: A mask does nothing about wet chemical on skin and clothing, and the ambulance entrance is still inside the building.

choices.text: Find gowns and gloves for yourself and then go meet them at the door.
choices.feedback: Personal protection is right, but standard gowns are not chemical protection and the decision to decontaminate outside must be made and communicated first.

steps.prompt: Two hours in, the department is holding. A woman comes to the desk asking whether her husband was on the bus. Several patients arrived unidentified and are carrying temporary alphabetic identifiers.

choices.text: Direct her to the designated family reunification area and notify the person running it, without confirming or denying anything about any patient.
choices.feedback: Correct. Reunification is a defined role during an incident precisely so that identification is verified and families are not told the wrong thing in a hallway.

choices.text: Walk her through the department to look at the unidentified patients.
choices.feedback: This breaches the privacy of every patient she walks past and risks a misidentification made under extreme stress.

choices.text: Tell her the department cannot give out any information and ask her to wait in the lobby.
choices.feedback: Accurate but incomplete. There is a defined place and person for this, and sending her to a lobby chair with no path is how families end up searching the corridors.

steps.prompt: The last patients are placed. The charge nurse says the department is still over capacity and asks for anything that will create beds.

choices.text: Offer to work the reverse triage list: move discharge-ready and least-sick patients out and turn over their rooms.
choices.feedback: Correct. Reverse triage is the named mechanism for creating capacity in a surge, and room turnover is the part a tech owns.

choices.text: Suggest putting new arrivals in hallway spots without telling anyone.
choices.feedback: Hallway beds are a real surge tool but they are assigned by the charge nurse, and unannounced placements leave patients unmonitored.

choices.text: Start a full reassessment round on every lobby patient.
choices.feedback: Reassessment must not be dropped, but at this moment the charge nurse asked for capacity. Say you will do both and get the round assigned rather than substituting one for the other.

scenarios.debrief: Surge work is not a different skill set, it is the ordinary one performed in a different order. Before patients arrive, capacity and staged supplies are the only things you can still create. During arrival, START inverts your instincts: ambulatory patients are green no matter how loudly they are suffering, the dramatic open fracture is yellow, and the quiet patient breathing at 36 with no radial pulse is the red. Contamination never comes through the doors, because a contaminated department stops being a department. Families go to a named reunification role, not to a hallway, because unidentified patients carry temporary identifiers precisely to prevent a wrong answer given under stress. And reverse triage is the formal name for the thing a tech actually does all afternoon: move the least sick out so the sickest have somewhere to go.
